docs.title: The Virtual Ecosystem Data Science Repository
docs.text:
This site documents how the Virtual Ecosystem (VE) model is parameterised, run and tested for specific field sites. It covers the data we use, the choices we make when turning that data into model inputs, and what the model results mean for those sites.

It is a companion to the main Virtual Ecosystem documentation. That site explains the model itself: the theory, the implementation and how to use the software. This site does not repeat that material and links to it wherever the model needs explaining.

docs.title: AI-assisted parameterisation
docs.text: The ve-constant-search skill helps find published values for Virtual Ecosystem (VE) configuration constants in any module, one or a few at a time. It produces proposals for human review, not validated parameters or automatic changes to VE. A model default or an abstract alone is not evidence for a new value.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
1. Open a workspace containing this repository and a sibling virtual_ecosystem repository. Use the VE version whose constants you want to assess; record its commit and any relevant uncommitted changes.
  2. Run uv sync from the repository root to install the Python dependencies declared in pyproject.toml, including jedi, tomli-w and requests. See Python with uv. For the optional R documentation lookup, run renv::restore() from the repository root to install the packages in renv.lock, including ragnar and DBI. Rebuilding the documentation store also needs tidyverse from that lockfile. Local renv use is otherwise optional; see R with renv.
  3. Configure OPENALEX_EMAIL with your own contact address. See the commands below. The address identifies API traffic to OpenAlex; it is not a password or API key.

docs.title: Configure OpenAlex
docs.text:
For repo-local setup, create .github/skills/ve-constant-search/.env with:

OPENALEX_EMAIL=you@example.org

Replace you@example.org with your address. The file is ignored by Git. The helper reads it relative to its own location, regardless of the working directory. No Positron restart is needed. It does not read R .Renviron files.

An existing OPENALEX_EMAIL in the process environment takes precedence over the .env file. To use the repo-local address instead, remove the user-level variable and restart Positron, or unset it in the terminal running the helper:

Remove-Item Env:OPENALEX_EMAIL

On macOS or Linux, use unset OPENALEX_EMAIL instead.

If you cannot provide an address, stop before searching. Do not switch to OpenAlex MCP tools or another search integration.

In an assistant that supports repository skills, ask it to use ve-constant-search. Name the constants or parameter families you want reviewed. For example:

Use ve-constant-search to review published values for the soil microbial turnover constants in this workspace. Show the search and source evidence, units, conversions and gaps before proposing any CSV changes.

Select one or a few qualified names (module.Class.attribute). If you name a module, class or family, agree on a small subset before searching. The example above is a soil-specific request, not the default scope.

docs.title: Review the evidence
docs.text:
The workflow has a review step before it saves results:

flowchart TD
    A[Select one or a few constants] --> B[Check VE source and inventory]
    B --> C{Units and model form clear?}
    C -- No --> D[Ask for clarification]
    D --> B
    C -- Yes --> E[Search and log candidates]
    E --> F{Eligible full-text evidence?}
    F -- Yes --> G[Check values, units and conditions]
    F -- No --> H[Record the evidence gap]
    G --> I[Discuss proposals and gaps]
    H --> I
    I --> J{User approves results?}
    J -- No --> K[Stop without changing results]
    J -- Yes --> L[Write module CSV and search log]
    L --> M[Check saved values against source and VE commit]

The search does not change VE configuration. A failed search cannot support a no_evidence result.

The assistant uses ve_constant_usage.toml to match selected constants to declarations, reference sites, functions and VE commit. This generated inventory covers declared configuration attributes across VE modules, including shared model and disturbance settings. It excludes hardcoded numeric literals and external trait tables. Reference resolution is best-effort. Review the VE declaration and reference sites directly for each selected constant. Resolve ambiguous units or functional forms before accepting an interpretation.

When the local VE commit changes, run the inventory dry run from this repository root with a clean VE package source tree:

uv run --no-sync python .github/skills/ve-constant-search/scripts/refresh_constant_metadata.py

Review listed added, removed and changed qualified names. Only then rerun with --apply to replace the TOML. The script skips a matching commit and rejects uncommitted VE package source changes. It uses the sibling VE clone by default; use --ve-root to point to another clone. Match the tool's Python environment to the selected local VE clone before regenerating: the generator imports VE configuration classes. Do not apply an inventory built from a different VE installation. Check changes outside the package that might affect imports separately. The TOML is generated model grounding, not empirical evidence. Updating it does not rerun literature searches or update historical reports. Do not assume a local full-text library exists.

Use only the Python helper for OpenAlex discovery and citation lookup. Do not use webfetch or general web search for literature discovery or screening. For screened candidates, webfetch is permitted only to open a specific full-text article or PDF URL identified by the helper or supplied by the user; do not use it to search for additional papers. For a PDF URL, check access and retention rights before optionally downloading it with:

uv run --no-sync python \
  .github/skills/ve-constant-search/scripts/download_authorized_pdf.py \
  "PDF_URL" "OUTPUT.pdf" --doi "DOI"

Use a specific HTTPS PDF URL returned by the OpenAlex helper or supplied by the user. Create the output directory first. Keep PDFs outside the repository unless retention there is permitted. The tool rejects redirects and non-PDF responses, never overwrites files, and saves a .pdf.json provenance record beside the PDF. A saved PDF still needs manual full-text review. If full text is inaccessible, record that gap instead of searching elsewhere.

For each candidate, expect a recorded search query and date, screened and excluded sources, and a traceable full-text quotation with a page or table location. Compare the original measurement's units, conditions, organism or enzyme source, and response function with the model. Check every conversion to model units. If a value requires re-fitting, digitising, pooling or other reanalysis, record it as a gap rather than a verified value; ask for approval before doing that reanalysis. Only use full text you are allowed to access and retain; an inaccessible paper, search failure or abstract-only result cannot verify a value. Citation counts do not establish measurement quality.

For soil microbial groups, seek separate evidence for bacteria, saprotrophic fungi, arbuscular mycorrhiza and ectomycorrhiza; soil enzymes need separate bacterial and fungal evidence. For other modules, check their applicable categories and measurement conditions. Missing groups remain gaps; do not fill them with pooled measurements. A no_evidence result describes the limits of this search, not proof that no literature exists.

docs.title: Approve and retain results
docs.text:
Discuss proposed values, exclusions and gaps before authorising changes. The assistant must ask before it uses proxies or changes inclusion criteria. It must also ask before it makes a consequential scientific judgment. After your approval, it writes results under data/derived/llm/, with one CSV per VE module: <module>_constant_literature_values.csv. For soil, create this CSV from the blank template for new searches. An older soil CSV exists at data/derived/soil/llm/soil_constant_literature_values.csv. That file contains historical results and is not the output path for new searches. Do not copy its rows into a new CSV without approval. Rows for other constants must remain unchanged. The skill's CSV template is blank; the field guide defines its fields. The historical soil CSV uses a different column order, so match columns by name if you review its rows. Keep each module's new results in its own CSV. Put each per-parameter log beside the corresponding module CSV.

Each supported value should identify its source, quotation, original units, conversion, measurement conditions and confidence. If only a range is supported, retain the range without inventing a point estimate. For gaps, record why the evidence is insufficient. Keep the search and screening log beside the resulting CSV so another reviewer can trace what was considered. Start a new per-parameter log from the blank log template. Record failed requests separately from successful zero-result searches. The OpenAlex helper supports search "QUERY" and snowball --id W... via uv run --no-sync python .github/skills/ve-constant-search/scripts/openalex_search.py from the repository root. It only returns candidates; it does not verify full text. Before using any proposal in VE, verify it against the cited source and the recorded VE commit. This workflow does not update VE configuration or historical parameterisation reports automatically.

docs.title: Abiotic validation plan
docs.text:
For each VE abiotic variable we find observations or published values, convert them to the VE unit and the VE monthly time step, record how close they are to the VE grid in space and time, for comparing them with the model output for the same cells and months.

This plan gives an overview of that process for the abiotic and abiotic simple modules at Maliau: the variables to validate and the data they need or still lack (Section 3), the data in hand (Section 4), how the data are processed (Section 5) and the status of each variable (Section 6).

File What it holds data/primary/validation/maliau_variables_summary.xlsx (globus) VE variables with unit and validation priority (output_variables) and model constants (model_constats) data/primary/validation/dataset/ (globus) The raw data from SAFE Zenodo: safe_abiotic/ (microclimate loggers, flux tower meteorology and eddy covariance) and safe_soil/ (soil temperature and moisture surveys; primary forest plots only are used) data/primary/validation/abiotic/abiotic_literature_values.csv (globus) Published values and ranges, one row per value, with citation, DOI and status data/primary/validation/abiotic/abiotic_sources.toml (globus) Where each dataset is, its columns, units, quality limits, coordinates, citation and screening record analysis/abiotic/validation/abiotic_validation_data.py (github) Python script that reads, cleans and converts the data, generates abiotic_validation_data.xlsx and writes the tracker in Section 6 data/derived/validation/abiotic/abiotic_validation_data.xlsx (globus) Processed data: daily and monthly values, the long table validation_long and the variable_registry (with the data needed or lacking per variable)

Derived variables combine VE outputs, or observations, so that they match each other. They are candidates for data/derived/validation/derived_variables.toml (step 5 of the validation database).

Derived variable Formula Unit vapour_pressure (observed) $e_a = e_s(T)\,RH / 100$, $e_s(T) = 0.6112 \exp(17.62\,T / (T + 243.12))$, the Magnus equation the VE uses (pyrealm calc_vp_sat, default coefficients of Sonntag 1990) kPa vapour_pressure_deficit (observed) $VPD = e_s(T) - e_a$ kPa latent_heat_flux from evapotranspiration $LE = ET \cdot \lambda$ / seconds per period (as calculate_latent_heat_flux in the VE), with $\lambda = 1.91846 \times 10^6\,(T_K / (T_K - 33.91))^2$ J kg⁻¹ (Henderson-Sellers 1984, as the VE; about 2.44 MJ kg⁻¹ at 25 °C); the evapotranspiration values of the hydrology plan also check LE W m⁻² energy balance closure $G = R_n + LE + H$ with the VE signs (see the sign convention below the table: $R_n$ positive when the surface gains energy, $LE$ and $H$ negative from the surface to the air, $G$ positive into the soil); in the VE the topsoil $G$ is this residual W m⁻² diurnal_temperature_range (observed) monthly mean of daily maximum − daily minimum air temperature °C above-canopy net_radiation, latent_heat_flux, sensible_heat_flux sum of the VE profile over the canopy layers, surface layer and topsoil, compared with the flux tower; the VE stores LE and H as negative from the surface to the air, so the tower LE and H change sign (obs_in_ve_unit) W m⁻²

Sign convention of the energy balance. The plan uses the VE signs for each term of the energy balance:

  • $R_n$ (net radiation) is positive when the surface gains energy, that is, it absorbs more radiation from the sun and sky than it emits.
  • $LE$ (latent heat flux) and $H$ (sensible heat flux) are negative when heat leaves the surface (soil or leaves) and goes into the air, and positive when heat goes from the air to the surface.
  • $G$ (ground heat flux) is positive when heat goes down into the soil.

With these signs the balance is $G = R_n + LE + H$: the soil receives the radiation energy the surface gains ($R_n$), less the energy used to evaporate water ($LE$) and warm the air ($H$). The VE computes the topsoil $G$ this way, as the residual. The SAFE flux tower reports $LE$ and $H$ as positive from the surface to the air, so obs_in_ve_unit holds them with the VE sign.

Inputs and constants the same data can check: the ERA5-Land forcing (air temperature, relative humidity, pressure and wind against the flux tower above the canopy); surface_albedo and leaf_albedo; the soil constants marked as placeholders in the code (soil_porosity, soil_thermal_conductivity_dry, soil_thermal_conductivity_saturated) through soil temperature at 5, 10 and 20 cm; and the leaf area index gradients in AbioticSimpleBounds (from Hardwick et al. 2015) through the loggers. Values are in the model_constats sheet.

Model inputs that the comparison also needs, beyond the validation data: leaf area index and canopy height for the maliau_2 cells (they set the VE layers and drive the abiotic simple gradients), latitude set to Maliau, and the logger and sensor heights to pick the matching VE layer.

docs.title: 7. Next steps
docs.text:
1. Choose the VE layer to compare with the loggers (1 m above ground).
  2. Extract the to_extract literature values.
  3. Agree the eddy covariance quality flag threshold (flux_qc_max, now 3). Few months pass the diurnal-course rule: 9 for latent heat flux, 23 for sensible heat flux and 26 for wind speed.
  4. Collect or derive the data in the data needed / lacking column. Three gaps can be closed with data already in hand: diurnal_temperature_range (logger and tower daily maxima and minima), atmospheric_co2 (co2_mole_fraction) and aerodynamic_resistance_canopy above the canopy (wind speed and friction velocity in SAFE_EC_byYear.xlsx).
  5. Check the termite control plots' soil moisture of about 2 % in the 2016-03 drought.

Points to agree on before comparing:

  • Where on the grid: every cell gets the same ERA5-Land forcing, so differences between cells come only from the land surface. Proposed: the grid mean against the mean of the Maliau old-growth loggers as the main target, the cells holding the OG2 plots as a check, and the spread across cells against the spread across plots as a test of spatial variation.
  • Which layer: the loggers are 1-1.5 m above the ground, and the VE has no layer at 1 m: the surface layer is at 0.1 m and the lowest canopy layer depends on the canopy. Proposed: the surface layer, with the lowest canopy layer as a check; not the reference height 2 m above the canopy.
  • Which model: compare abiotic and abiotic simple in the same way?
  • The logger period (2013-2019) and the flux tower period (2012-2018) are inside the run (2010-2020); the SAFE plots and the flux tower are regional checks only.
  • Monthly means of one modelled day: the VE value is the mean of one 24-hour day built from the monthly forcing, so compare it with the mean of the month's mean diurnal course (as the script does for the flux tower), not with single days.
  • Flux tower height: the tower measures 25-27 m above the canopy, higher than the VE reference height (2 m above the canopy), so above-canopy air temperature, humidity and wind are a range check only.

Possible model issues found while reading the code (inferred from the code, not yet tested; to raise with the VE developers before reading the results):

  • Day length: the daily cycle uses 12 + 4 cos((month − 1) π / 6) cos(latitude) hours, which at Maliau gives about 16 hours in January and 8 hours in July instead of about 12 hours all year.
  • Shortwave radiation in the modelled day: fixed in the current model code (the hourly weights are now multiplied by 24, so the day's mean equals the monthly mean).
  • Diurnal temperature range: the forcing range is used as the amplitude of the temperature sine curve, so the modelled day spans twice that range.
  • abiotic simple net radiation has no incoming longwave term, and its longwave emission is calculated from the temperature in °C, not kelvin (calculate_longwave_emission expects kelvin; the abiotic model adds 273.15), so the emission is close to 0 W m⁻² and net radiation is close to the absorbed shortwave.

docs.title: Animal-model validation plan
docs.text:
This is a draft plan for validating the animal model outputs in the VE project with the help of Copilot. It is intended to be a living document that will be updated as the model and its outputs evolve, as well as new validation datasets are identified. Currently, the document is written for Maliau and SAFE scenarios.

Notes:

  • Perhaps some of the sections can be split into smaller sections or subsections with fewer variables?

docs.title: 1. Scope and rules
docs.text:
1. Animal-model validation only, including cross-module outputs when they directly support animal interpretation.
  2. Validation metrics are computed from exported outputs and post-processing only.
  3. Targets are organised into a) site-specific emergent or derived targets and b) global emergent pattern checks (Madingley based).

docs.title: 2. Secondary validation targets (emergent or derived from outputs)
docs.text: Targets in this section are site-specific.

docs.title: 2.1 Population and biomass density structure by functional group
docs.text:
Derivation: Derive post-model population density and biomass density from functional group abundance, occupancy, territory, and elemental mass.

Inputs: individuals, functional_group, occupancy_proportion, territory_size, mass_carbon, mass_nitrogen, mass_phosphorus, is_mature.

Validation approach: Compare equilibrium density ranges and biomass density against published empirical datasets in Maliau or SAFE. Stratify by body-mass class and diet class where available.

TODO: Align with Arne how we approach verifying against spatially variable density.

Datasets needed: Site-level abundance or density datasets, biomass density datasets, including live-mammal trapping data from Chapman et al. (2018), camera-trap data from Wearn et al. (2016) and Wearn et al. (2017), and the 2011-13 density estimate from Wearn et al. (2022). Sarah Luke has termite density data https://zenodo.org/records/1198833. Sri Rao's thesis (PDF) includes earthworm density data https://zenodo.org/records/3857210. For the above and other invertebrates, we have the Maliau Quantitative Inventory https://zenodo.org/records/5562260.

TODO: contact Ollie Wearn and Phil Chapman.

docs.title: 2.2 Nutrient-return flux contributions from animals
docs.text:
Derivation: Excrement and carcass proxies from consumed stoichiometry, assimilation efficiency assumptions, and mortality estimates.

Inputs: decomposed_excrement_cnp, decomposed_carcasses_cnp, herbivory_waste_leaf_cnp, C, N, P, cohort_id, time_index, is_alive, individuals.

Validation approach: Compare decomposed excrement, carcass loss, and herbivory waste fluxes against empirical nutrient-return studies and litterfall or carcass-decomposition datasets.

Datasets needed: Excretion datasets, carcass decomposition studies, nutrient-return studies, and herbivory waste measurements. Sui has carcass decomposition data from Danum and oil palm plantations and can be used only if appropriate and if we find a solution for the spatial mismatch.

docs.title: 2.3 Aggregated consumption partitions
docs.text:
Derivation: Aggregate trophic interaction records and consumption partitions to habitat-, guild-, or functional-group-level rates and proportions, then compare those derived quantities with observed energetic sums and assimilation.

Inputs: resource_kind, C, N, P from animal_trophic_interactions.csv; animal_pom_consumption_cnp, animal_bacteria_consumption, animal_saprotrophic_fungi_consumption, animal_ectomycorrhiza_consumption, animal_arbuscular_mycorrhiza_consumption, litter_consumed_above_metabolic_cnp, litter_consumed_above_structural_cnp, litter_consumed_woody_cnp, litter_consumed_below_metabolic_cnp, litter_consumed_below_structural_cnp, total_animal_respiration, decomposed_excrement_cnp, decomposed_carcasses_cnp, mass_carbon, mass_nitrogen, and mass_phosphorus.

Validation approach: Compare derived functional-group-level consumption sums and assimilation energetics against published datasets. For the Malhi supplementary tables, use AnimalGroup_Habitat as the habitat key when matching food-group energetics, because the ForestType labels in MOESM7_ESM__Energetics_byFoodGroup.csv are internally inconsistent for logged versus old-growth forest rows.

Datasets needed: Resource-specific intake studies, assimilation efficiency datasets, animal energy-budget studies, stoichiometric balance datasets. For example,

1) Malhi supplementary habitat-, guild-, and food-group energetics tables. 2) Josh Twinning thesis on energy flows in beetles. Email for raw data.

docs.title: 2.4 Coupled plant-animal productivity linkage
docs.text:
Derivation: Animal intake and biomass response versus plant productivity, plant allocation, and plant-supported intake ratios.

Inputs: canopy_foliage_cnp, subcanopy_vegetation_biomass, plant_ammonium_uptake, plant_nitrate_uptake, plant_phosphorus_uptake, canopy_foliage_cnp_consumed, canopy_seed_cnp_consumed, canopy_fruit_cnp_consumed, subcanopy_vegetation_cnp_consumed, subcanopy_seedbank_cnp_consumed, mass_carbon, individuals, functional_group, occupancy_proportion, territory_size.

Validation approach: Compare modelled site animal intake from section 2.3 as a fraction of plant productivity (NPP) against observed energetic intake as %NPP from the Malhi NPP by plot tables. Plant ammonium, nitrate, and phosphorus uptake are already exported as areal daily uptake rates, so no rooting-depth conversion is required.

Datasets needed: Plant productivity datasets, herbivory impact datasets, coupled plant-animal interaction studies. Malhi supplementary has NPP kJm^-2 day^-1 (5 SAFE plots, 2 Maliau plots, 1 oil palm plot) and habitat energetics tables.

docs.title: 2.5 Space-use and territory-use realism
docs.text:
Derivation: Build occupancy-weighted territory and location-use summaries by cohort and functional group through time.

Inputs: occupancy_proportion, territory_size, centroid_key, territory, location_status, individuals, functional_group, time_index.

Validation approach: Compare occupancy and territory-use distributions, persistence, and movement signatures against telemetry, home-range, and territory-use datasets for comparable taxa and body-size classes.

Datasets needed: Home-range studies, telemetry datasets, territory-size summaries, and movement ecology datasets. Wearn et al. (2022) estimated home ranges from camera-trap data, and the Brasington (2019) thesis estimated small-mammal home ranges from live-mammal trapping. Estimates from both sources are at species and site level.

docs.title: 3. Global validation relationships (Madingley emergent pattern checks)
docs.text: These are all much lower priority than site-specific validation. Targets in this section are global and not specific to any site. Bracketed numbers in this section refer to the numbered source references used by Harfoot et al. (2014) to support each comparison dataset.

docs.title: 3.1 Body mass versus growth rate
docs.text:
Relationship type: Individual-level allometric scaling.

Inputs: cohort_id, time_index, age, mass_carbon, mass_nitrogen, mass_phosphorus, largest_mass_achieved.

Reference anchor: Harfoot et al. (2014), Figure 3A.

Validation approach: Compare emergent growth-rate scaling against observed growth data for terrestrial vertebrates and invertebrates.

Datasets needed: Growth datasets for reptiles, mammals, birds, and terrestrial invertebrates from Case (1978), Ricklefs (1968, 1973), and related compiled sources [46–48]. Where growth rates were derived from body length, use the length-mass conversions cited by Harfoot et al. [58–61].

docs.title: 3.2 Body mass versus time to maturity
docs.text:
Relationship type: Individual-level allometric scaling.

Inputs: time_to_maturity, largest_mass_achieved, is_mature.

Reference anchor: Harfoot et al. (2014), Figure 3B.

Validation approach: Compare modelled age at maturity against published maturation datasets and check that larger-bodied cohorts mature later.

Datasets needed: Maturation and life-history datasets for invertebrates, reptiles, mammals, and birds [49–53,57], with length-mass conversions where necessary [58–60].

docs.title: 3.3 Body mass versus mortality rate
docs.text:
Relationship type: Individual-level allometric scaling.

Inputs: cohort_id, time_index, is_alive, individuals.

Reference anchor: Harfoot et al. (2014), Figure 3C.

Validation approach: Compare estimated mortality scaling against published natural mortality datasets and inspect whether the model reproduces the observed decline in mortality with increasing body mass.

Datasets needed: Natural mortality datasets for invertebrates, mammals, and birds from terrestrial mortality compilations and trait syntheses.

docs.title: 3.4 Body mass versus lifetime reproductive success
docs.text:
Relationship type: Individual-level allometric scaling.

Inputs: cohort_id, time_index, is_mature, reproductive_mass_carbon, reproductive_mass_nitrogen, reproductive_mass_phosphorus.

Reference anchor: Harfoot et al. (2014), Figure 3D.

Validation approach: Compare predicted lifetime reproductive success against trait and demographic datasets, checking for the broad body-mass scaling seen in the paper.

Datasets needed: Mammal, bird, and insect reproductive success datasets compiled from PanTHERIA, bird reproductive studies, and insect life-history studies [63–71].

docs.title: 3.5 Biomass density and abundance-density scaling
docs.text:
Relationship type: Community-level allometric scaling.

Inputs: mass_carbon, individuals, functional_group, occupancy_proportion, territory_size.

Reference anchor: Harfoot et al. (2014), Figures 4B, 4D, and S5.

Validation approach: Compare density-body-mass slopes and biomass density of the whole community (instead of only large herbivores) against observed community assemblages.

Datasets needed: Biomass and abundance estimates, and terrestrial assemblage abundance-density datasets. Malhi et al. (2022) provides biomass for plants and vertebrate animals for reconstruction; additionally, we add invertebrate biomass data from section 2.1.

docs.title: 3.6 Biomass pyramids and herbivore:producer ratios
docs.text:
Relationship type: Community-level trophic structure.

Inputs: mass_carbon, mass_nitrogen, mass_phosphorus, individuals, functional_group, canopy_foliage_cnp, subcanopy_vegetation_biomass.

Reference anchor: Harfoot et al. (2014), Figure 4A and 4C, Tables S3 and S5.

Validation approach: Compare terrestrial biomass pyramids and herbivore-to-producer biomass ratios against geographically located terrestrial ecosystem summaries.

Datasets needed: Aggregated animal biomass data from section 3.5 and plant biomass from Malhi et al. (2022).

docs.title: 5.4 Derivation formulas for emergent targets
docs.text:
The derivation formulas below were generated by Copilot and should be reviewed.

Notation:

  • $i$: cohort index
  • $g$: functional group index
  • $c$: grid-cell index
  • $t$: timestep index
  • $\Delta t$: timestep duration in days
  • $A_c$: area of grid cell $c$ in m$^2$
  • $N_{i,t}$: individuals for cohort $i$ at time $t$
  • $w_{i,t}$: occupancy_proportion for cohort $i$ at time $t$
  • $m^e_{i,t}$: per-individual cohort mass of element $e \in {C,N,P}$

Effective abundance in a cell:

$$ N^{eff}{i,t} = N{i,t} \cdot w_{i,t} $$

Functional-group density (for 2.1, 3.5):

$$ D_{g,c,t} = \frac{\sum_{i \in (g,c)} N^{eff}_{i,t}}{A_c} $$

Element-specific cohort biomass and functional-group biomass density (for 2.1, 3.5, 3.6):

$$ B^e_{i,c,t} = N^{eff}{i,t} \cdot m^e{i,t} $$

$$ \rho^e_{g,c,t} = \frac{\sum_{i \in (g,c)} B^e_{i,c,t}}{A_c} $$

Cohort growth rate (for 3.1):

$$ G^e_{i,t} = \frac{m^e_{i,t+1} - m^e_{i,t}}{\Delta t} $$

and relative growth rate:

$$ g^e_{i,t} = \frac{m^e_{i,t+1} - m^e_{i,t}}{m^e_{i,t} \cdot \Delta t} $$

Trophic intake aggregation from interaction records (for 2.3 and 2.4):

$$ I^e_{c,t} = \sum_{k \in (c,t)} e_k $$

Per-day intake rate:

$$ \dot{I}^e_{c,t} = \frac{I^e_{c,t}}{\Delta t} $$

Soil consumption volumetric-to-areal conversion (for 2.2, 2.3):

$$ F^{e,areal}{c,t} = F^{e,vol}{c,t} \cdot z_{soil} $$

with $z_{soil}$ as the active soil depth in metres.

Plant-supported intake ratio for plant-animal productivity linkage (for 2.4):

$$ Q_p = \frac{I^{plant}_p}{NPP_p} $$

where $I^{plant}_p$ is plot-level intake from plant-derived resources and $NPP_p$ is plot-level net primary productivity, matching the spatial resolution of the Malhi plot-level NPP data. Plant ammonium, nitrate, and phosphorus uptake are already exported as areal daily rates, so no rooting-depth conversion is required for this comparison.

Occupancy-weighted territory size and resident persistence (for 2.5):

$$ \bar{T}{g,c,t} = \frac{\sum{i \in (g,c)} \left(w_{i,t}\cdot territory_size_{i,t}\right)} {\sum_{i \in (g,c)} w_{i,t}} $$

$$ P^{res}{g,c,t} = \frac{\sum{i \in (g,c)} \mathbf{1}(location_status_{i,t}=\mathrm{resident})}{n_{g,c,t}} $$

Nutrient return flux to soil (for 2.2):

$$ NR^e_{c,t} = decomposed_excrement_cnp^e_{c,t} + decomposed_carcasses_cnp^e_{c,t} + \frac{herbivory_waste_leaf_cnp^e_{c,t}}{A_c} $$

Biomass pyramid and herbivore:producer ratio (for 3.6):

$$ B^{C}{H,c,t} = \sum{i \in H} N^{eff}{i,t} \cdot m^C{i,t} $$

$$ B^{C}{P,c,t} = canopy_foliage_cnp^{C}{c,t} + subcanopy_vegetation_biomass_{c,t} $$

$$ R_{H:P,c,t} = \frac{B^{C}{H,c,t}}{B^{C}{P,c,t}} $$

For 3.6, use animal biomass aggregates derived in 3.5 and pair them with plant biomass aligned to Malhi et al. (2022).

Allometric density scaling regression (for 3.5):

$$ \log D_{g,c,t} = \alpha + \beta \log \bar{M}_{g,c,t} + \varepsilon $$

For 3.5, apply this scaling to whole-community cohorts across functional groups, not a large-herbivore-only subset.

where $\bar{M}_{g,c,t}$ can be represented by mean largest_mass_achieved or mean carbon mass per individual in group $g$.

docs.title: 6. Notes on references and implementation boundaries
docs.text:
1. Non-Madingley targets should prioritise SAFE-linked empirical references during implementation, with target-specific citations added as the validation database is populated.
  2. Madingley-style emergent checks should use Harfoot et al. (2014) as the core pattern-validation anchor.
  3. All calculations in this plan are post-processing targets and should be implemented without changing ecological process code unless a required output is unavailable.
  4. Defer validation of reproduction, survival and mortality rates as we do not have detailed demographic models at the moment. This may be possible with advanced statistical models such as the Cormack-Jolly-Seber (CJS) model.
  5. Defer validation of activity-window and respiration as there are no data and these checks can be circular. TODO: confirm whether camera-trap data should be used for diel activity estimates in functional-group parameters.
  6. Defer this global relationship check: there is no significant productivity gradient between SAFE and Maliau. If we include Silwood, we can consider reopening it.
  7. Reject global biomass-pattern checks because they can be easily overwritten by local dynamics.

docs.title: Derived and emergent variables from the Virtual Ecosystem
docs.text:
Hao Ran Lai

The Virtual Ecosystem outputs data variables according to the model specifications, such as soil carbon in separate pools (e.g., organic vs microbial). In practice, ecologists tend to measure total carbon amount in their soils, and therefore they would need to manipulate the simulation's output data to match empirical measurements.

We call the variables that are transformations, aggregations or summaries of the original output variables as "derived variables".

docs.title: Functions to calculate derived variables
docs.text:
Tip

This is a growing section. We expect to include more derived variables as we develop the Virtual Ecosystem. Currently there is only R functions, but we expect to have python functions soon.

Currently, we derive variables using custom post-processing scripts. To try it out, load the functions:

# load dependencies
box::use(tools/R/R/get_data_variables[...])

# load the actual function to derive variables
box::use(tools/R/R/get_derived_variables[...])

We are using box::use() in place of source() to load a function, because the functions have been documented in Roxygen2 formats that can be viewed using box::help(get_derived_variables).

We expect you to usually do get_derived_variables(<path to model_data.zarr>, <path to compiled configuration TOML>), which returns a list of derived-variable arrays. See box::help(get_derived_variables) for a specific example using the maliau_2 scenario.

docs.title: Getting the repository

The first step is to clone the repository. If you do not already have git then you will need to install it:

docs.title: Github Overview
docs.text:
Important

This is currently a draft document

Github is an online platform for code sharing and collaboration. Multiple developers can work on a project at once, make changes on their own copy of the code (called a "branch"), get feedback on the changes from other team members, and then "merge" their changes into the core code-base. This page walks you through basic git and github functionality used for the project.

docs.title: Lingo
docs.text:
• Repository (repo): the codebase.
  • Branch: a copy of the codebase where local changes don't immediately impact the main branch
  • Commit: a package of changes that you're satisfied with, and then group them together and label with a description.
  • Pull request: a functioning chunk of code that can be safely merged into the main codebase without breaking any other functionality
  • Push: send your commits to the upstream version of your branch (the online version)

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
1. Make a github account and login.
  2. Find the repository that you want to work on. Click on the green "code" button and copy the link under clone.
    • If your github account usees two-factor authentication or single sign-on you will need to use the SSH version, otherwise you can use HTTPS.
    • If you use the SSH version, your computer will need to communicate with github automatically to authenticate you when you make changes from your desktop. To do this you need to generate a SSH key and add it to your GitHub account.
  3. Decide where you want the repo to be stored on your local computer. Open a terminal window and navigate to this location (cd FOLDERNAME moves you into a folder, and cd .. moves you backwards.)
  4. Once you have found the folder, paste git clone SSH/HTTPS REPO URL into the terminal. This should download a copy of the up-to-date code into your local computer.
  5. Open VS Code (or another processor such as PyCharm) and open the folder that you just downloaded.

You can now add files, make changes, and work on the codebase. Once you're ready to share those changes, go to the next section!

docs.title: Checkout a new branch
docs.text:
By default, when you download the code you will be on the main branch. This branch includes all the approved code. Never work directly on the main branch - you should always create your own branch, and merge it into main only later once the code is ready and has received approval.

  1. Check what branch you're on. VS Code has the name of the branch in the bottom left, or you can run git branch in the terminal.
  2. Pull the most recent version of main. Before you create a new branch, make sure your main is up-to-date. This will be the copy of the code that you start from. To pull, use the refresh button in the bottom left of VS Code, or run git pull in the terminal.
  3. Create a new branch. You can create a new branch in VS Code by clicking on the branch name and then the "Create a new branch..." option that should show up. Otherwise, run git checkout -b BRANCH NAME in the terminal. Your branch name doesn't need to be long, but should be descriptive enough so that you remember what you're doing on it in case you switch between branches.

docs.title: Commit and push your code
docs.text:
Committing your code is a way to package up some changes that should all be logically grouped together and describing what you've done. A commit is a helpful way for other developers to quickly look at the change you've made with the intention you had, so that they can easily review the changes.

  1. First, check exactly what changes git has tracked. This ensures that you don't commit anything you don't mean to (like old work, commented out code, etc.) You can do this in VS Code in the "Source Control" tab. Anything labelled "changes" is work that hasn't yet been marked as ready to add to a commit. Anything labeled "staged changes" includes work that you have indicated is ready to commit, but has not yet been committed.
  2. Check over your changes and stage them. Click on the files under changes and look through what has been added (will be noted with blue highlight next to the line numbers). As long as you are happy, you can stage the changes by clicking the "+" button next to the file.
  3. Once you are ready to commit all your staged changes, press the blue commit button. This will open a new file where you can type a commit message (a brief description of what work has been done). Then, click the check mark button.
  4. Push your changes to github. To send your changes to github, press the "publish" button. This sends a copy of the work on your branch to github, so anyone can see what you have been doing.

You can also perform these tasks from the terminal window if you prefer. Some basic commands are git status to see what branch you're on and what files have changed; git diff to see what your changes are; git add FILENAME to stage changes in that file; git commit -m COMMIT MESSAGE to commit all the staged changes; and git push to push your changes to github.

docs.title: Creating a pull request and merging
docs.text:
1. Once you are ready for a code review (and ultimately for your code to be merged into the main branch), go on github and create a pull request (PR). You can do this from the pull request tab, or if you've recently pushed from a local branch, github will prompt you to make a PR from that branch. When you're making a PR, you want to merge your branch into main.

  2. Add a description of what the PR accomplishes and request review from the relevant team members.

  3. Wait for the reviews to come in: it makes life hard for reviewers if there are more changes coming into a PR while they are trying to review it!

  4. Respond to reviews. Your reviewers can either give approval or request changes. Even if they approve the PR, they may also make some comments for minor changes, so before merging (see below) you should go through any comments in the review and deal with them. Typical actions are:

  5. Making some additional changes on the branch to address the comment and then commiting and pushing those changes.

  6. Accepting a "suggestion" - this option appears when a reviewer has posted some actual changes, a bit like a suggestion in track changes in Word, rather than a comment about what they would like you to change. You can accept suggestions directly in GitHub but will then need to use git pull to bring those suggestions into your local copy

  7. Simply replying to the comment - it might be that the comment just wanted clarification without needing to changes anything, or it might be that there are good reasons not to do what the comment asks. This might involve a short discussion before deciding on what to do.

When a comment has been handled, it is good practice to leave some form of comment: that could just be a simple "thumbs up" reaction for simple changes or could be a few sentences explaining what you've done. You should click on the "resolve conversation" button when there is no further action to be taken.

If a reviewer has requested changes, you will need to request a new review from that reviewer to get them to approve the update PR.

  1. Once you have approvals from all reviewers, you can merge from the PR page, which sends your updates into the main branch. If the main branch has changed since you started your branch and PR, you may need to update the branch before you can merge.

  • Always create new branches off of main. Go into VS Code (or the terminal) and switch to the main branch. Pull the latest version before creating a new branch.

docs.title: Running Virtual Ecosystem on the HPC
docs.text:
Author: moi-taiga

Introduction to submitting Virtual Ecosystem runs as a PBS array job on the HPC cluster. The workflow was developed for the CX3 cluster, which uses the PBS job scheduler. CX3 is scheduled to be shut down in May 2027.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need:

  • a terminal;
  • access to CX3

docs.title: Connect to the HPC using SSH
docs.text:
Use SSH to access the cx3 cluster; you will be required to use your password for authentication.

ssh userid@login.cx3.hpc.imperial.ac.uk

See the Imperial RCS documentation for further information about connecting to the cluster. If you are new to HPC environments, do make sure that you familiarise yourself with the documentation. It is highly recommended to attend the Introduction to HPC at Imperial course , but if you cannot make it, the materials for the course are freely available and give a good overview of how to work with the system.

Importantly: Login nodes are intended for tasks such as editing files, preparing jobs, and submitting jobs. Computationally intensive work should be submitted to compute nodes through PBS.

docs.title: Clone the repository
docs.text:
The project datafiles are shared via GLOBUS from the path:

/rds/general/project/virtual_rainforest/live/ve_data_science/

This directory is also the root for a clone of the ve_data_science repository but it is really important that this clone is kept up to date and on the main branch. This ensures that the code files available through GLOBUS are synchronized with the data files they run.

For this reason, you must use a personal checkout of the ve_data_science repository into your own user directory to run code. This is like using the local clone on your own computer: it isolates the code you are running from other users and also avoids altering the code files served through GLOBUS.

cd ~
git clone https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/ve_data_science.git
cd ve_data_science

Traceability and code versions

When you run code on the HPC, you need to be able to trace the outputs back to the versions of any ve_data_science code being used and the version of Virtual Ecosystem being run. The Virtual Ecosystem will include version information in the output log but you need to ensure that you are using specific named releases and then documenting which releases were used.

For the ve_data_science code this means taking care to check which branch is currently checked out: you are likely to be using the current code in main.

docs.title: Install uv and create a virtual environment
docs.text:
See uv setup for instructions about using uv. Note that by default uv is configured to use the most recent release on PyPi, but you can specify to run using the most recent code by setting --group dev to alter the uv dependency group with the uv sync and uv run commands below.

uv venv
uv sync

docs.title: Install the example data/configs
docs.text:
For testing the HPC workflow, install the example data and configuration files:

uv run ve_run --install-example .

docs.title: Create a array job configuration
docs.text:
Create a TOML job specification that describes the Virtual Ecosystem runs in the array. You can produce the job entries with a sampling method such as Morris, Sobol, or Latin hypercube sampling. A small example is available in hpc_jobs/example_hpc_configs/arrayJob_config.toml.

The specification has four parts:

  • site_directory: the absolute path to the directory containing the shared configuration files and input data. Replace the path in the example with the path to your checkout's ve_example directory.
  • common_config_paths: paths to configuration files, relative to site_directory, that every array sub-job uses.
  • [[subJobs]]: one or more job entries. Each can provide additional config_paths and a cli_config table of values that override the loaded configuration.
  • repeats: a positive integer on each job entry. The total number of PBS array sub-jobs is the sum of all repeats values.

docs.title: Submit the PBS array job
docs.text:
The submission script takes three arguments:

  1. the array job configuration TOML file;
  2. the PBS resources configuration TOML file (see Choose job resources);
  3. a new output directory for the completed array run.

The output directory must not already exist. The script creates it and then creates one child directory per PBS array sub-job. From the repository root, run:

uv run python -m hpc_jobs.submit_ve_array_job \
    hpc_jobs/example_hpc_configs/arrayJob_config.toml \
    hpc_jobs/example_hpc_configs/pbs_resources_config.toml \
    ve_example/<experiment-output>

The submission script loads and validates both TOML configuration files using Pydantic. By default, it also validates each Virtual Ecosystem configuration before creating the requested output directory, and submitting the array using qsub. It creates an array_subJob_<index> directory for each sub-job. Validation happens before the output directory is created or any jobs are submitted, so invalid configurations fail fast.

For known-good Virtual Ecosystem configurations, add --skip-ve-validation to skip their model-level validation:

uv run python -m hpc_jobs.submit_ve_array_job \
    hpc_jobs/example_hpc_configs/arrayJob_config.toml \
    hpc_jobs/example_hpc_configs/pbs_resources_config.toml \
    ve_example/<experiment-output> \
    --skip-ve-validation

This option does not skip loading, TOML parsing, or Pydantic validation of the array job and PBS resources configuration files.

docs.title: Monitor jobs
docs.text:
Use PBS commands to inspect or cancel jobs:

List your active jobs:

qstat -u "$USER"

Inspect a completed job:

qstat -x -f <job_id>

Cancel a job:

qdel <job_id>

Each array sub-job receives an array_subJob_<index> directory. The combined PBS standard output and standard error are written to pbs.log; the Virtual Ecosystem log is written to ve.log, and model outputs are written in the same directory:

ve_example/<experiment-output>/
    array_subJob_1/
        pbs.log
        ve.log
        compiled_configuration.toml
        model_data.nc

hpc_jobs/run_subJob.py does not write these files directly to the sub-job's output directory. Virtual Ecosystem writes its outputs (including the intermediate Zarr store) to a staging directory under the compute node's local $TMPDIR. Once the run completes, the Zarr store is deleted, and the remaining files (the NetCDF conversion, compiled configuration, and logs) are moved into the sub-job's array_subJob_<index> directory. This keeps the large number of small files generated by the Zarr store off shared/quota-limited storage entirely.

docs.title: Choose job resources
docs.text:
The PBS resource request is defined in a resource configuration TOML file. hpc_jobs/example_hpc_configs/pbs_resources_config.toml has a small allocation suitable for the example data.

Every value applies to each individual array sub-job, apart from max_concurrent_jobs, which caps how many sub-jobs the scheduler runs at once.

Larger datasets may require more memory, CPUs, or wall time. More jobs don't need more resources as resources are set per job.

hpc_jobs/parse_resources_config.py loads and validates the resource configuration, while hpc_jobs/parse_arrayJob_config.py loads and validates the array job configuration. Each resource field is bounds checked, and an out-of-range value aborts the submission with an error rather than sending a bad request to qsub:

Field Allowed range ncpus 1–128 mem_gb 1–4000 walltime_hours 0–59 walltime_minutes 0–59 max_concurrent_jobs 1–100

The upper bounds match the largest CX3 nodes rather than realistic per-job requests, so staying inside them does not guarantee that a job will be scheduled promptly. Check the Imperial RCS documentation for more detail.

docs.title: Manage file quotas
docs.text:
Each array sub-job now produces a small, fixed set of output files (pbs.log, ve.log, compiled_configuration.toml, model_data.nc, and any per-model CSV outputs) because the Zarr store, which previously generated approximately 3,600 files per sub-job, is written to the compute node $TMPDIR space and deleted once the NetCDF conversion completes. It is never copied to shared storage. This reduces the file-count pressure on HPC storage quotas for large array runs.

Check your current usage with:

quota

docs.title: Hydrology validation plan
docs.text:
For each VE hydrology variable we find observations or published values, convert them to the VE unit and the VE monthly time step, record how close they are to the VE grid in space and time, for comparing them with the model output for the same cells and months.

This plan gives an overview of that process for the hydrology module at Maliau: the variables to validate and the data they need (Section 3), the data in hand (Section 4), how the data are processed (Section 5) and the status of each variable (Section 6).

Inputs and constants the same data can check: the precipitation forcing (against the gauges), saturated_hydraulic_conductivity, soil_moisture_saturation, soil_moisture_residual and the van Genuchten parameters (values in the model_constats sheet). Two constants already look out of range for Maliau:

  • saturated_hydraulic_conductivity is 3.5 × 10⁻⁵ m s⁻¹ in VE, 5 to 57 times the values measured at Danum (6.1 × 10⁻⁷ to 7.1 × 10⁻⁶ m s⁻¹, in hydrology_literature_values.csv).
  • soil_moisture_residual is 0.175, so VE soil cannot be drier than 17.5 %. A quarter of the soil respiration readings are below 18.2 %, so the driest observed months cannot be matched.

Snow variables and constants are left out: there is no snow at Maliau.

Checks against the raw files and the papers (2026-10-13): monthly runoff, rainfall, soil moisture and the storm-event totals recalculated from the raw files match the workbook. The record means agree with Nainar et al. (2018, Fig. 4): runoff ratio 0.62 against 0.615 at VJR and 0.77 against 0.789 at PF; rainfall 2920 and 3529 mm against 2904 and 3504 mm. The Lyne-Hollick baseflow index (0.43 at both) matches the paper's Hewlett-Hibbert value at VJR (0.42) but not at PF (0.68), so read baseflow with the method in mind. PF runoff is high for the Danum station rainfall (some months with more runoff than rain; P − Q about 800 mm per year), as in the source. The termite survey readings of March 2016 (about 2 %) look too low for these soils.

Every row is then classed by its distance to the grid and its period:

docs.title: 7. Next steps
docs.text:
1. Confirm the meaning of "% of pore space" in the soil respiration dataset and the probe depth of the termite survey.
  2. Extract the Danum matric potential values (Newbery and Lingenfelder 2022).
  3. Look for a continuous soil moisture record and a river gauge at Maliau.

Points to keep in mind when comparing: 2010-2013 is spin-up in current runs and overlaps the stream records; the probes measure 0-12 cm, the upper half of the VE top layer; the stream gauges are 64-94 km from the grid and drain larger catchments, so compare monthly totals and specific discharge, not storm peaks. VE splits the monthly rainfall at random over the days of the month (wet and dry days drawn with a fixed seed), so daily and storm-scale values from VE do not match real days; use monthly values only. Compare sums with sums (runoff, rainfall, fluxes) and means with means (discharge rate, soil moisture).

docs.title: Plant validation Overview
docs.text:
Each row summarizes one observed-predicted variable pair. For exact extents, entries in the spatial and date lists are aligned by position; repeated plot or cell labels represent separate matches.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Sensitivity analysis (SA) evaluates how uncertainty in model parameters propagates to model outputs and quantifies the relative importance of model parameters. It provides a systematic framework for understanding model behaviour, identifying influential parameters, supporting uncertainty quantification, and guiding model calibration (Saltelli et al., 2004; Pianosi et al., 2016).

For the Virtual Ecosystem (VE), sensitivity analysis helps to:

  • identify influential parameters;
  • rank parameter importance;
  • quantify parameter interactions;
  • detect nonlinear model behaviour;
  • reduce parameter dimensionality before calibration;
  • prioritise field measurements;
  • support uncertainty analysis.

Sensitivity analysis is particularly important for complex ecosystem models because their behaviour is often nonlinear, involves interactions between parameters, and represents multiple interconnected physical and biological processes (Pianosi et al., 2016).

docs.title: Local versus Global Sensitivity Analysis
docs.text: Sensitivity analysis methods are generally classified into local and global approaches.

docs.title: Local Sensitivity Analysis (LSA)
docs.text:
Local sensitivity analysis evaluates the effect of changing one parameter around a single point in parameter space, typically a calibrated parameter set.

Characteristics:

  • one parameter varied at a time;
  • computationally inexpensive;
  • ignores parameter interactions;
  • suitable for preliminary model diagnostics.

Typical methods include:

  • One-at-a-Time (OAT);
  • finite difference methods;
  • derivative-based approaches.

Local sensitivity analysis is useful for simple models but becomes less representative for highly nonlinear systems because it only explores a small region of the parameter space (Saltelli et al., 2004; Pianosi et al., 2016).

docs.title: Global Sensitivity Analysis (GSA)
docs.text:
Global sensitivity analysis evaluates parameter importance across the entire parameter space.

Unlike local methods, all parameters vary simultaneously, allowing nonlinear responses and parameter interactions to be quantified.

Characteristics:

  • explores the complete parameter space;
  • captures nonlinear behaviour;
  • accounts for parameter interactions;
  • provides robust parameter rankings;
  • requires substantially more model evaluations.

Global sensitivity analysis is generally recommended for hydrological and ecosystem models because these systems exhibit complex interactions between parameters and processes (Pianosi et al., 2016).

docs.title: Common Global Sensitivity Analysis Methods
docs.text:
Several approaches are available for global sensitivity analysis.

Method Category Captures interactions Computational cost Typical application One-at-a-Time (OAT) Local No Very low Model debugging Morris Screening Partial Low Initial parameter screening Sobol Variance-based Yes High Detailed sensitivity analysis eFAST Variance-based Yes Moderate Alternative to Sobol Regression-based Statistical Limited Low Linear models PAWN Density-based Yes Moderate Distribution-based analysis Random Forest Machine learning Implicit Moderate Large simulation datasets

For the Virtual Ecosystem, the Morris and Sobol methods are currently implemented using the SALib Python library. Morris provides efficient parameter screening, while Sobol performs a rigorous variance decomposition of model outputs (Saltelli et al., 2004; Wang & Solomatine, 2019).

docs.title: Morris Method
docs.text:
The Morris method, also known as the Method of Elementary Effects, is a computationally efficient screening technique designed to identify influential parameters within high-dimensional parameter spaces (Morris, 1991).

Rather than providing exact variance contributions, Morris estimates the overall importance of each parameter using repeated elementary effects calculated across the parameter space.

docs.title: Morris Outputs
docs.text:
• μ — mean elementary effect;
  • μ* — mean absolute elementary effect (overall parameter importance);
  • σ — variability of elementary effects, indicating nonlinear behaviour or parameter interactions.

docs.title: Morris Advantages
docs.text:
• computationally efficient;
  • suitable for large parameter sets;
  • identifies influential parameters quickly;
  • ideal before calibration.

docs.title: Morris Limitations
docs.text:
• qualitative rather than quantitative;
  • interaction effects are inferred indirectly;
  • does not provide variance decomposition.

The Morris method has been widely applied in hydrological modelling as an efficient first-stage screening tool before more computationally intensive methods are applied (van Griensven et al., 2006; Zhan et al., 2013).

docs.title: Sobol Method
docs.text:
Sobol analysis is a variance-based global sensitivity analysis method that decomposes model output variance into contributions from individual parameters and their interactions (Sobol, 2001).

Unlike Morris, Sobol provides quantitative sensitivity indices and explicitly measures parameter interactions.

docs.title: Sobol Outputs
docs.text:
• S₁ — first-order sensitivity index;
  • S₂ — second-order interaction index;
  • ST — total-order sensitivity index.

docs.title: Sobol Advantages
docs.text:
• quantitative parameter ranking;
  • captures parameter interactions;
  • suitable for highly nonlinear models;
  • regarded as one of the most rigorous global sensitivity analysis methods.

docs.title: Sobol Limitations
docs.text:
• computationally expensive;
  • requires substantially more model evaluations;
  • less practical for large parameter sets without prior screening.

Sobol analysis is widely regarded as one of the most comprehensive methods for quantifying parameter importance in nonlinear environmental models (Sobol, 2001; Saltelli et al., 2004).

docs.title: Morris versus Sobol
docs.text:
Feature Morris Sobol Method type Screening Variance decomposition Parameter ranking Qualitative Quantitative Parameter interactions Indirect Explicit Computational cost Low High Suitable for many parameters Yes Limited Recommended stage Before calibration Detailed analysis

Comparative studies consistently recommend Morris for efficiently identifying influential parameters with relatively few model evaluations, while Sobol is better suited for detailed quantitative analysis once the parameter space has been reduced (van Griensven et al., 2006; Wang & Solomatine, 2019; Zhan et al., 2013).

docs.title: Python Sensitivity Analysis Workflow
docs.text:
The current Python workflow implements global sensitivity analysis for the Virtual Ecosystem hydrology module. However, the workflow has been designed to be modular and reusable, allowing the same pipeline to be adapted for other Virtual Ecosystem modules (e.g. abiotic, soil, plant, animal and litter) by providing the appropriate parameter definitions and base configuration files.

The implemented workflow currently covers parameter definition, sample generation, and creation of HPC job configurations required to execute batch simulations runs.

The workflow consists of the following stages.

Define parameter ranges
    │
    ▼
Load parameter definitions
    │
    ▼
Generate parameter samples
(Morris / Sobol)
    │
    ▼
Generate HPC job configuration
(job_config.toml)
    │
    ▼
Submit HPC batch jobs
    │
    ▼
Run batch HPC simulations
    │
    ▼
Future work
(Output extraction, sensitivity analysis and reporting)

docs.title: Step 1. Define parameter ranges
docs.text:
Parameter names and sampling bounds are defined in

sensitivity_parameters.toml

Each parameter is identified using its full Virtual Ecosystem configuration key (for example,

hydrology.constants.groundwater_capacity)

together with lower and upper sampling bounds.

docs.title: Step 1 Files
docs.text: data/sensitivity/hydrology/config/sensitivity_parameters.toml

docs.title: Step 1 Purpose
docs.text:
The parameter definition file specifies:

  • parameter groups (e.g. hydrology, soil, abiotic);
  • Virtual Ecosystem configuration keys;
  • lower and upper sampling bounds.

Adding a new module simply requires defining a new parameter group within sensitivity_parameters.toml.

docs.title: Step 2. Load parameter definitions
docs.text:
The helper function

load_problem(...)

reads the selected parameter groups and constructs a SALib-compatible problem definition containing:

  • parameter names;
  • sampling bounds;
  • number of variables.

docs.title: Step 2 Tool
docs.text: tools/python/abiotic/sensitivity_tools.py

docs.title: Step 2 Output
docs.text:
problem = {"num_vars": ..., "names": ..., "bounds": ...}

This problem dictionary is then passed directly to SALib sampling routines.

docs.title: Step 3: Generate parameter samples
docs.text:
Parameter samples are generated using either

generate_morris_samples(...)

or

generate_sobol_samples(...)

implemented using the SALib Python package (Herman & Usher, 2017; Iwanaga et al., 2022).

docs.title: Step 3 Tool
docs.text: tools/python/abiotic/sensitivity_tools.py

docs.title: Step 3 Driver scripts
docs.text:
analysis/abiotic/sensitivity/morris_sample.py

analysis/abiotic/sensitivity/sobol_sample.py

docs.title: Step 3 Output
docs.text: The generated sample matrix contains one parameter combination per simulation.

docs.title: Step 4. Generate HPC job configuration
docs.text:
The sampled parameter combinations are converted into a Virtual Ecosystem job_config.toml file using

generate_job_config(...)

Each sampled parameter set becomes one independent Virtual Ecosystem simulation.

docs.title: Step 4 Tool
docs.text: tools/python/abiotic/job_config_tools.py

docs.title: Step 4 Input files
docs.text:
The base configuration provides the default Virtual Ecosystem model settings. Only the sampled parameters are overridden for each simulation.

data/sensitivity/hydrology/config/hydrology_base_config.toml

docs.title: Step 4 Output
docs.text:
data/sensitivity/hydrology/config/job_config_sobol.toml

or

data/sensitivity/hydrology/config/job_config_morris.toml

These job configuration files define the sensitivity analysis simulations and are intended to be used by the Virtual Ecosystem HPC batch workflow to execute ensembles of model runs. Each [[jobs]] entry represents a single simulation with a unique set of sampled parameter values.

docs.title: Step 5: Execute Virtual Ecosystem simulations (planned)
docs.text:
This stage is currently under development and has not yet been implemented. Once the sensitivity sampling workflow is complete, the generated job_config.toml files will be submitted through the Virtual Ecosystem HPC batch workflow to execute the sensitivity analysis experiments.

job_config.toml
        │
        ▼
PBS job array
        │
        ▼
Multiple Virtual Ecosystem simulations

Each [[jobs]] entry represents one simulation with a unique parameter set.

docs.title: Step 6: Post-processing sensitivity analysis (planned)
docs.text:
This stage has not yet been implemented and represents the next phase of the sensitivity analysis pipeline.

Following successful execution of the HPC simulations, a post-processing workflow will be developed to:

  • extract Virtual Ecosystem model outputs;
  • aggregate model outputs across simulations;
  • compute Morris elementary effects (μ, μ*, σ);
  • compute Sobol sensitivity indices (S₁, ST and S₂);
  • rank influential parameters;
  • identify parameter interactions;
  • generate figures, tables and summary reports.

The completed workflow will support interpretation of sensitivity results and provide a basis for selecting parameters for subsequent calibration and validation.

The planned implementation will make use of the SALib analysis routines (SALib.analyze.morris and SALib.analyze.sobol) (Herman & Usher, 2017; Iwanaga et al., 2022).

docs.title: Recommended Strategy
docs.text:
For the Virtual Ecosystem, a staged sensitivity analysis strategy is recommended.

Morris screening
        │
        ▼
Reduce parameter set
        │
        ▼
Sobol analysis
        │
        ▼
Calibration
        │
        ▼
Model validation

This staged workflow combines the computational efficiency of Morris with the rigorous variance decomposition of Sobol, reducing computational cost while retaining robust parameter ranking and interaction analysis (van Griensven et al., 2006; Wang & Solomatine, 2019; Pianosi et al., 2016).

docs.title: SALib
docs.text:
The Virtual Ecosystem sensitivity analysis workflow is implemented using SALib, an open-source Python library for global sensitivity analysis (Herman & Usher, 2017).

SALib currently provides implementations of:

  • Morris;
  • Sobol;
  • FAST;
  • eFAST;
  • PAWN;
  • Delta;
  • DGSM;
  • Fractional Factorial Sampling.

As sensitivity analysis becomes a core capability of the Virtual Ecosystem, SALib is expected to become a core project dependency managed using the project's uv environment, ensuring consistent package versions across local development, continuous integration and HPC system.
